# Draft:Norwegian invasion of Bohuslän (1711)

The Norwegian invasion of Bohuslän (, ) more commonly referred to as '''Løvendal's Feud''' (, ) was fought from  21 August to 16 September 1711 during the Great Northern War between Sweden and Denmark–Norway. To divert the attention of the Swedes from the war in Northern Germany, the commander-in-chief of Norway, Woldemar Løvendal, was ordered to march across the Svinesund and invade the Swedish province of Bohuslän.
Background
200
Having been forced out of the Great Northern War by the Treaty of Travendal in 1700, Denmark–Norway re-entered the war against Sweden in late 1709, following the defeat of King Charles XII at the Battle of Poltava. Subsequently, a Danish army of some 14,000 men invaded and occupied much of Scania, but was decisively defeated by Magnus Stenbock at the Battle of Helsingborg in early 1710. In late September 1709,  was appointed commander-in-chief of Norway. He was ordered to march across the Svinesund
Prelude
150 words
For the defense of Bohuslän and Dalsland, Burensköld had four regiments at his disposal, with a few other companies stationed around Kviström and Uddevalla. In total, these probably numbered between 1,500 and 1,700 men.
Invasion
August
250 words
Orders were issued to break camp on 20 August. In the early hours of the 21st, the main column under Hausmann crossed the Svinesund, while Lützow’s column of around 1,200 men crossed the Iddefjord from . Simultaneously, near  dragoons under Captain Hans Adam Stockman drove off a Swedish party under Colonel Petter Ingelsson Weinholtz sent to reconnoiter the Norwegian advance, which fell back toward the Vättelanda Bridge. Upon Weinholtz’s return, Colonel Thure Bielke, who was positioned north of Vättelanda, ordered the Vättelanda Bridge to be burnt and withdrew with his four dragoon companies to Rabbalshede. Warned by Bielke of the Norwegian advance, Burensköld rode to , where he assembled the available units and appealed to Stenbock in Scania for reinforcements.
The following day, Løvendal arrived at the headquarters in Skee, by which time the two columns had already united just south of the village. Løvendal sought to cut off Bielke's retreat; however, Cicignon's flotilla was unable to reach  due to the poor weather. Nonetheless, the Norwegians then proceeded towards Vättelanda Bridge, which was rebuilt on the 23rd. In the meantime, Burensköld had withdrawn to Dingle, where on the 24th he redeployed several units to defend Kviström and Uddevalla. The Norwegians set up camp at Tanum on the 25th, prompting Burensköld to withdraw to Herrestad and then Uddevalla.
September
On the 15th, Løvendal convened a council of war, where it was decided that the army would retreat. He had also received inaccurate reports claiming that the Swedish army had been reinforced to 11,000 men. At dawn the next day, the baggage train was ferried across the Svinesund, the rest of the army following in its wake until, by evening, the entire force had crossed and the pontoon bridge over the Svinesund was destroyed. Burenskiöld began dispersing the army on his own initiative before orders from the Riksrådet arrived; he stayed to oversee the final defensive transition until departing for Stockholm on 30 October.
